rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community asking why the Sabbath-breakers are admonished comprised passive bystanders who neither protested nor themselves profaned the Sabbath.
rows.anchor: people who, while not actively protesting against the impiety of their environment, did not themselves participate in this profanation of the Sabbath.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who answer are the truly pious among the community, like those described in 7:159.
rows.anchor: the really pious among them, such as are described in verse 159 above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saved group is described literally as those who were forbidding evil.
rows.anchor: who were forbidding the evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their expectation of forgiveness despite pursuing worldly gain reflects a persistent belief that descent from Abraham guarantees divine forgiveness and grace regardless of their conduct.
rows.anchor: no matter what they do, His forgiveness and grace are assured to them by virtue of their being Abraham's descendants.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the claim of forgiveness as an erroneous belief that pardon can be gained without sincere repentance.
rows.anchor: A reference to their erroneous idea that God's forgiveness could be obtained without sincere repentance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine writ referred to twice in this passage is the Bible.
rows.anchor: The divine writ mentioned twice in this passage is obviously the Bible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shaking of the mountain may refer to an earthquake when the Law, or tablets, were revealed to Moses.
rows.anchor: which took place at the time of the revelation of the Law

rows.speaker: Taj al-'Arus
rows.claim: Taj al-'Arus glosses ta'if and its forms as an elusive phantom, image, or suggestion, including an obsession that obscures the mind.
rows.anchor: "an imperceptible obsession which obscures the mind" (Taj al-'Arus).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the suggestion comes from Satan, Asad considers dark suggestion an apt rendering of ta'if.
rows.anchor: Since, in the above context, it is described as coming from Satan

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib explains that God can intervene between a person's desires and their outward action, turning the person away from the heart's urge.
rows.anchor: God can turn man away from what his heart urges him to do (Raghib).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God-consciousness alone prevents wrongful desires from misleading a person and making them like those who do not reason.
rows.anchor: it is God-consciousness alone that can prevent man from being misled by wrong desires and, thus, from becoming like

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to what gives life means spiritual awareness of right and wrong together with the will to act on it.
rows.anchor: that is, spiritual awareness of right and wrong and the will to act accordingly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr, the Prophet and his followers camped at the valley's northern end nearest Medina, while the Meccans occupied its southern end.
rows.anchor: the Prophet and his followers were encamped in the northern part of the valley of Badr, nearest to Medina

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caravan was Abu Sufyan's Meccan trade caravan from Syria, traveling south through the coastal lowlands.
rows.anchor: The Meccan trade caravan, coming from Syria under the leadership of Abu Sufyan, was in the meantime proceeding southwards through the coastal lowlands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad freely expands the elliptical conditional: had they arranged a battle appointment, they would have failed to keep it.
rows.anchor: a very free rendering of the elliptic phrase which runs, literally, thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most followers expected to meet the relatively weak trade caravan, and some were dismayed to face the powerful Quraysh army instead.
rows.anchor: most of the Prophet's followers had been under the impression that their objective was the relatively weak trade caravan

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: All commentators take Asad's bracketed additions as implied by the highly elliptical sentence.
rows.anchor: According to all the commentators, the words interpolated by me between brackets are implied

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A decree of God must inevitably come to pass, so the verse can describe it as already done.
rows.anchor: meaning that if God decrees a thing, it must inevitably come about

words: لِّيَهْلِكَ مَنْ هَلَكَ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ وَيَحْيَىٰ مَنْ حَىَّ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ
rows.speaker: Some of the great commentators
rows.claim: Some major commentators read destruction as continued denial of truth and life as faith, metaphorically.
rows.anchor: Some of the great commentators understand this sentence in a metaphorical sense

words: لِّيَهْلِكَ مَنْ هَلَكَ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ وَيَحْيَىٰ مَنْ حَىَّ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ
rows.speaker: Ibn Ishaq
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq, quoted by Ibn Kathir, reads the phrase as allowing deniers to persist in denial and believers in belief after clear evidence.
rows.anchor: Ibn Ishaq, as quoted by Ibn Kathir

words: لِّيَهْلِكَ مَنْ هَلَكَ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ وَيَحْيَىٰ مَنْ حَىَّ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers the literal deaths and survival of Badr's participants: fallen believers knew themselves martyrs, survivors saw God's hand in victory, and defeated deniers saw the futility or cause of their defeat.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, however, it is preferable to interpret the references to death and life in their prima-facie (that is, not metaphorical) sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These people are neither full believers nor hypocrites, but hesitant and confused between right and wrong or truth and falsehood.
rows.anchor: half-hearted, confused waverers between right and wrong, or between truth and falsehood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as confessing sins after mixing a righteous deed with an evil one.
rows.anchor: who have acknowledged their sins [after] having mingled a righteous deed with another that was evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse primarily concerns wavering Muslims who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition.
rows.anchor: vacillating Muslims who refused to participate in the expedition to Tabuk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, it applies to any sinners who recognize and repent of wrongdoing without outside prompting.
rows.anchor: all sinners who - without external prompting - become conscious of their wrongdoing and repent of it.

rows.speaker: Razi and Manar XII, 161
rows.claim: Razi and Manar XII, 161 explain the exception as God willing to give the people of Paradise a still greater reward.
rows.anchor: God wills to bestow on them a yet greater reward (Razi; also Manar XII, 161)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad considers it more probable that the exception means God opens for humanity a new and higher stage of evolution.
rows.anchor: which to my mind is more probable - unless He opens up to man a new, yet higher stage of evolution.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the opening particle law-la as alas, referring readers to his note on 10:119.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of the particle law-la, at the beginning of this sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage follows the statement that God requites good-doers in 11:115 and that everyone receives their due in 11:111.
rows.anchor: The present passage connects with the statement in the preceding verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on 6:5 for the broader implications of qarn, rendered generation.
rows.anchor: For the wider implications of the term garn ("generation"), see surah 6, note 5.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tarifa means enjoying ease and plenty; mutraf describes someone enjoying or indulging in such a life.
rows.anchor: while the participle mutraf denotes "one who enjoys a life of ease and plenty" or "indulges in the pleasures of life"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutarraf adds that ease and comfort can make a person insolent or corrupt through the exclusive pursuit of pleasure, explaining Asad's rendering.
rows.anchor: The form mutarraf has an additional significance, namely, "one whom a life of softness and ease has caused to behave insolently"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his note 65 on surah 6 for related explanation.
rows.anchor: See surah 6, note 65.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muta'al occurs only once in the Qur'an, here.
rows.anchor: which occurs in the Qur'an only in this one instance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attribute denotes God's infinite exaltedness above everything existing or possible.
rows.anchor: denotes His infinite exaltedness above anything existing or potential

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari adds that God is above anything that human definitions can circumscribe.
rows.anchor: according to Zamakhshari, above anything that could be circumscribed by human definitions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawl primarily means a saying or utterance, but can figuratively mean an idea whether spoken or merely conceived; here it means unspoken thoughts.
rows.anchor: Since in the above verse this term obviously refers to unspoken thoughts, I have rendered it accordingly.

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, as cited by Baghawi and Razi, interprets going forth by day as committing evil deeds openly.
rows.anchor: commits evil deeds openly (Ibn 'Abbas, as quoted by Baghawi and Razi)

rows.claim: Asad directs readers to Appendix II and his note on surah 11:1 for discussion of the opening letters.
rows.anchor: See Appendix II; also surah 11, note 1.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's prayer presents recognition of God's existence, oneness, and uniqueness, and rejection of belief in other powers, as the path to righteousness.
rows.anchor: recognition of God's existence, oneness and uniqueness and, hence, a rejection of all belief in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer expresses gratitude for God's bounty and links back to 14:34 and forward to 14:42.
rows.anchor: it connects directly with the preceding verse 34 and the subsequent verse 42.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The land in Abraham's prayer is where the Kaaba stands, specifically Mecca.
rows.anchor: I.e., the land in which the Kabah is situated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asnam, translated idols, is not limited to concrete images of false deities.
rows.anchor: asnam, sing. sanam) does not apply exclusively to actual, concrete representations of false

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says shirk can include worshipful devotion to causal agencies and outward means such as wealth, power, luck, or people's favor.
rows.anchor: Razi points out, in a worshipful devotion to all manner of "causative agencies and outward means to an end"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True monotheism divests the heart of attachment to such agencies and recognizes no real directing power besides God.
rows.anchor: genuine faith in the oneness and uniqueness of God (at-tawhid al-maha) consists in divesting oneself of all inner attachment to [such] causative agencies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham accepts God's verdict in 2:124 concerning sinners among his descendants.
rows.anchor: Thus, Abraham accepts God's verdict (given in 2:124) regarding the sinners from among his descendants.
